In Java 8, the language underwent a paradigm shift by allowing interfaces to contain implementation logic, breaking the long-standing rule that interfaces must be purely abstract contracts. Default methods, denoted by the 'default' keyword, allow developers to provide a concrete implementation directly within an interface. This was primarily introduced to solve the 'Interface Evolution Problem.' Before Java 8, adding a new method to an interface would break every single class implementing that interface, as they would all fail to compile until the new method was implemented. By providing a default implementation, library maintainers can evolve APIs—such as the Java Collections Framework—without breaking binary compatibility for millions of existing downstream implementations.

Static methods in interfaces, conversely, serve as utility entry points that belong to the interface itself rather than an instance. Before this feature, developers were forced to create 'companion classes' (e.g., Collection vs Collections) to house static helper methods. By allowing static methods directly in the interface, we achieve cleaner namespace organization and better cohesion, keeping related utility logic physically closer to the interface definition.

items: Default methods utilize the 'invokespecial' bytecode instruction, allowing them to be called on interface instances without requiring an explicit implementation in the concrete class.
When a class implements multiple interfaces that define the same default method signature, the compiler forces an explicit override to resolve the 'Diamond Problem' ambiguity.
Static interface methods are not part of the object's VTable (Virtual Method Table), meaning they are resolved at compile-time and do not support polymorphic dispatch.
Default methods are often used to implement 'optional' operations in functional interfaces, allowing classes to only implement the methods they actually care about.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'gotcha' for seniors is the interaction between default methods and the Object class. You cannot provide a default method that overrides a method from java.lang.Object (like toString or equals). The JVM will ignore the default method because the implementation in Object is guaranteed to exist for every class, and the compiler enforces this to prevent unpredictable behavior in the class hierarchy.
